title: Red ochre

names.note: Also 'wet season'. Roth (1901) recorded kambar for the Bloomfield white kaolin.

scientificName: Iron-oxide earths (haematite, ferruginous clay); kaolin (white clay)

identification.basis: The dictionary names each material directly (red ochre, yellow ochre, streaky yellow ochre, white clay), and Roth (1901) independently recorded kambar as the Bloomfield name of white kaolin clay. Which deposits each word was applied to is not recorded.

summary: **[Murbuy](word:murbuy)** and **[wuba](word:wuba)** are red ochre. **[Makirr](word:makirr)** is yellow ochre, **[makarra](word:makarra)** 'streaky yellow ochre' and **[kambar](word:kambar)** 'white clay' [ref:hershberger1982]. Together with charcoal, these earths were the paint box of the Bloomfield. They were used for painting the body for hunting, fighting, mourning, initiation and dance, and for striping [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) handles red and white [ref:anderson1996]. Red ochre was something the Bloomfield people **produced and traded**, and yellow ochre came in by trade [ref:roth1910b14]. White clay was even made into a baked cake and eaten as a delicacy [ref:roth1901]. Ochre and clay pits can be culturally significant places and are protected as Aboriginal cultural heritage [ref:qld-acha].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
The dictionary gives two words for red ochre, **[murbuy](word:murbuy)** and **[wuba](word:wuba)**. It gives **[makirr](word:makirr)** 'yellow ochre', **[makarra](word:makarra)** 'streaky yellow ochre' and **[kambar](word:kambar)** 'white clay' [ref:hershberger1982]. *[Kambar](word:kambar)* also means 'wet season' [ref:hershberger1982]. The dictionary does not say why the clay and the season share a name.

Roth confirms *[kambar](word:kambar)*. In 1901 he wrote the Bloomfield name for the white kaolin clay as *[kambar](word:kambar)*, exactly as the dictionary spells it today [ref:roth1901]. *[Wuba](word:wuba)* is shared with the Guugu Yimithirr of Cape Bedford. Roth recorded *wo-ba* there for a red pigment of burnt ferruginous sandstone from the McIvor River. Their word for 'red' was *woba-dir*, literally 'with *woba*' [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body:
Ochres are natural earth pigments. Roth sorted the North Queensland pigments by colour [ref:roth1904]:

- **White.** Kaolin or pipe-clay, a fine white clay (hydrous silicate of alumina). He found it at the Bloomfield, at Cooktown and Cape Bedford, on the Palmer and elsewhere.
- **Red.** Oxides of iron. These include haematite (on the Palmer River), burnt ferruginous sandstone (McIvor River), red oxide probably made by burning yellow ochre (Pennefather River), and ferruginous clay with sand.
- **Yellow.** A yellow iron-oxide ochre with a little fine sand, traded from the north. It was said to be dug from under salt pans and dried in the sun.
- **Black.** Charcoal, 'used everywhere'.

On the Bloomfield the paints were **red and yellow ochres, Grevillea charcoal and white kaolin clay** [ref:anderson1996]. *[Makarra](word:makarra)*, the 'streaky' yellow, presumably names a banded or mottled ochre [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Where it is found
sections.body:
On the Bloomfield the white clay, *[kambar](word:kambar)*, was 'dug out from the veins in the cliffs or in the banks of the creeks' [ref:roth1901]. Red ochre came from Bloomfield country itself, since it was one of the district's own products for trade. Yellow ochre was mostly brought in [ref:roth1910b14]. The exact pits are not named in the published sources. Their locations are knowledge held by Traditional Owners.

**Western Yalanji country.** Inland, the Koko-minni of the middle Palmer River obtained red haematite together with burnt ferruginous clay, and called it *norda* [ref:roth1904]. Western Yalanji, a dialect of Kuku Yalanji, is the language of the wider Maytown, Mitchell and Palmer River area [ref:fca2013]. Painted caves and tools there show that Aboriginal people have lived in that region for at least 21,000 years [ref:fca2013]. The pigment trade linked the coast and the inland. Bloomfield and Endeavour River people travelled towards the Laura River and supplied the Koko-warra with red ochre and white clay [ref:roth1910b14].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Ochre moved in the trading season. Roth wrote that for the Bloomfield people, 'the principal time of barter was during the laying-season at King's Lake country', whenever there was enough food to draw people together [ref:roth1910b14]. Anderson places King's Lake country at King's Plains, near the Laura–Cooktown road [ref:anderson1996]. White clay cakes needed six to eight days of sun-drying before baking [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Body painting.** On the Bloomfield, body paint was put on for some hunting trips and for mourning, fighting, initiation and dancing. 'While men were painted anywhere on their bodies, women were only painted on the faces' [ref:anderson1996]. Roth also recorded that Bloomfield painting differed with the purpose: mourning, fighting, initiation or corroboree [ref:roth1910b15]. These are ceremonial matters, and the designs belong to their owners.

**Weapons and things.** [Spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) handles 'were usually painted with red and white stripes' [ref:anderson1996]. The white clay was also 'employed for painting weapons' [ref:roth1901]. On the Bloomfield the oil of the [candlenut](entry:candlenut), **[bilar](word:bilar)**, was 'used in fixing the ochre for spear-painting' [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1901]. The wheel for the spear-throwing game was covered on its sides with red clay and [beeswax](entry:native-bees) and decorated with feathers [ref:anderson1996]. Women's waist circlets of hair or fibre were prized when 'some red colour is woven into it' [ref:anderson1996].

**Food and medicine.** White clay was eaten at the Bloomfield and at Cooktown, 'as a food and as a medicine' [ref:roth1904]. It was prepared into a baked cake 'considered a delicacy' (see below) [ref:roth1901]. The outer crust of ant-hills, which Roth wrote as *kappai*, was eaten as a filler 'when no other edible substance is available' [ref:roth1901].

**Trade.** Bloomfield trade goods included [dilly-bags](entry:dilly-bags), spears, woomeras, gum-cements, edible pipe-clay (in recent years) and **red ochre**. In return came stingray spears, shell ornaments, **yellow ochre** and, in the old days, edible pipe-clay [ref:roth1910b14]. Small precious things like pigment travelled rolled up in [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark) and tied with [twine](entry:string-and-twine) [ref:roth1904].

**Meaning.** Roth found that across North Queensland white was 'essentially the colour of mourning', while red was the colour of force and energy, 'a man's colour', seen on warriors and fighting gear [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: How it was prepared
sections.body:
**Edible white clay cake, Bloomfield River** (R. Hislop to Roth) [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Dig the white clay** (*[kambar](word:kambar)*) from the veins in a cliff or creek bank.
2. **Pound it carefully and sift it** until it is quite smooth and free of grit.
3. Put it in a **bark trough** and work it with water into **a stiff paste**.
4. **Shape the paste into a cake.**
5. **Dry it in the sun for six to eight days.**
6. **Wrap it in leaves, bury it in the ashes and make a hot fire over it.**
7. When it has cooled it is ready to eat.

**White paint** (Palmer River and Cape Bedford, neighbouring peoples) [ref:roth1904]:

1. **Hammer the clay to a fine powder** between [stones](entry:stone).
2. **Mix it with water.**
3. **Dry it in the sun** and keep it for use. On the Palmer and Pennefather it was also used just as found.

**Paint that lasts, Bloomfield River** [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Grind the ochre or clay fine.
2. Mix it with **[candlenut](entry:candlenut) (bilar) oil**, the Bloomfield fixing medium for spear-painting. Spittle and water were the everyday media across the north.
3. Paint it on. [Spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) handles were striped red and white.

**Making red from yellow.** Elsewhere in the north, red was made by burning. On the Pennefather the red oxide was probably obtained by burning yellow ochre, and the Gunanni burnt their red pigment *marcla* before use [ref:roth1904]. No Bloomfield record says whether *[makirr](word:makirr)* was burnt to make *[murbuy](word:murbuy)*.

sections.heading: Safety and respect
sections.body: The clay-eating recipe above is a historical record, not a tested recipe or a recommendation [ref:roth1901]. More important: **ochre and clay sources can be significant cultural places**, and the paints themselves are tied to mourning, initiation and other ceremony [ref:anderson1996]. Do not dig, collect or use ochre from country without the Traditional Owners' permission. Anyone carrying out an activity in Queensland must take all reasonable and practicable measures not to harm Aboriginal cultural heritage [ref:qld-acha].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Queensland's *Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Act 2003* protects significant Aboriginal areas and objects and imposes a **cultural heritage duty of care** on everyone carrying out an activity [ref:qld-acha]. The Daintree, Ngalba-bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks were returned to Eastern Kuku Yalanji Traditional Owners in 2021 and are jointly managed with the Queensland Government [ref:qld-handback]. Inland, the Western Yalanji determinations of 2013 define the 'Natural Resources' native title holders may take and use to include 'any clays, soil, sand, gravel or rock'. Minerals under the *Mineral Resources Act 1989* are excluded [ref:fca2013]. Under s 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, native title holders may gather and carry out cultural activities for personal, domestic and communal needs without licences [ref:alrc-s211]. Visitors need Traditional Owners' permission.
